newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Feb inflation eases, Buba rates steady.
newsitem.headline: German Feb inflation eases, Buba rates steady.

text.p: A slowdown in German inflation in February, coupled with a government report saying Bonn saw no inflationary dangers, on Thursday reinforced economists' views that Bundesbank interest rates would stay steady for some time.
Pan-German consumer prices rose 0.4 percent in February from the month before to stand 1.7 percent higher than the same month a year ago, the Federal Statistics Office reported.
That is slightly lower than in January, when inflation was 1.8 percent compared to the previous year, but still higher than the levels seen throughout most of 1996.
The Wiesbaden-based statistics office also revised downward preliminary consumer price data it releases for west Germany -- based on figures from the four most populous states.

West German final consumer price data showed a rise of 0.3 percent in February from the month before and 1.7 percent year-on-year. Preliminary data had showed a rise of 0.4 percent and 1.8 percent. East German consumer prices rose 0.4 percent from January and 1.7 percent from a year ago.
While the recent weakness of the mark against the dollar has led to higher import prices, the Economics Ministry said in its monthly economic report there was no danger of inflationary pressure.

The recent strength of the dollar and seasonal factors in international commodities markets have led to limited increases in producer and consumer prices, but there is no reason to fear this will result in a broadening of inflationary trends.

"The price climate in Germany remains unusually favourable," it said. "Room for domestic price increases remains limited, and unit wage costs, the most important domestic cost component, are retreating."
"The consumer price index in February rose slighlty less than is typical for this time of year," it added.

The Bundesbank left official interest rates unchanged on Thursday. The discount rate, the floor on interest rates, was left at 2.50 percent and the Lombard emergency financing rate, the ceiling on rates, at 4.50 percent.
The central bank's main money market rate, the repo, was also kept steady at a fixed rate of three percent.

Few economists had expected the Bundesbank to take action on the headline rates, held steady since April 1996, since economic data this week showed modest growth and minimal inflation and supported the case for stable interest rates.

Growth in M3 money supply, the Bundesbank's top indicator, which had surged to an alarming 11.7 percent in January, slowed to 9.1 percent in February as strong bond markets tempted investors to move funds into long-term investments.
The closely-watched west German Ifo business climate index also edged up to 93.6 in February from 93.3 the previous month, providing more evidence of an improvement in the economy.

And as Germany battles with record post-World War Two unemployment, growth is still seen as far too restrained to sustain a rate increase. On the other hand, money supply growth remains too robust to justify easing rates, economists said.
The Economics Ministry added in its report that the economy remains in an uptrend, adding that it sees no reason to change its forecast of 2.5 percent economic growth in 1997.
"Recent developments give no grounds for a correction of the (projected) real growth rate of 2.5 percent on which the government's annual report on the economy is based," it said.
Upward forces such as low interest rates, stable prices, the stabilisation of the mark against the dollar and a dynamic world economy will rapidly regain the upper hand, the report added.
